meta.title: Who really said "First I Brush My Teeth and Then I Sharpen My Tongue"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Dorothy Parker. Quote Investigator traces the line to the pianist-wit Oscar Levant in a September 1940 Hollywood column; the Parker credit begins in the 2000s.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'First I Brush My Teeth and Then I Sharpen My Tongue'?
meta.ogDescription: Oscar Levant said it, in a syndicated column dated 26 September 1940. The Dorothy Parker credit was attached decades later, with nothing behind it.

answer.label: Not Dorothy Parker — actually Oscar Levant
answer.authorDates: 1906–1972 · American concert pianist, composer, actor and professional wit
answer.sourceLine: The quip belongs to Oscar Levant. Quote Investigator ↗ finds it first in the Hollywood columnist Erskine Johnson’s “Hollywood Today” of 26 September 1940 — where Levant’s surname is misspelled “Lavant” — and concludes that “Oscar Levant can be credited with the statement in the 1940 citation. The linkage to Dorothy Parker was spurious.” Four further 1940s printings all name Levant. Parker’s name does not appear on the line until the 2000s.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Erskine Johnson’s “Hollywood Today,” Santa Cruz Evening News, p. 5, col. 2
Oscar Levant — his surname set as “Lavant” in that first printing

source.excerpt: Asked about his morning routine by an interviewer, Oscar Lavant cracked: “First I brush my teeth and then I sharpen my tongue.”
trail: Quote Investigator’s article on this quip ↗ is the anchor. It dates the earliest known printing to 26 September 1940, in the Santa Cruz Evening News, and states its conclusion plainly: Levant is to be credited, and “the linkage to Dorothy Parker was spurious.”

QI then lists four further 1940s citations, every one of them naming Levant: Walter Winchell ↗’s column in December 1941; Sheilah Graham ↗ in September 1946, reporting that Levant used the line in a letter to the actor John Garfield; the Reader’s Digest of December 1946; and Evan Esar’s Dictionary of Humorous Quotations of 1949.

Independently of QI, Wikiquote’s Oscar Levant page ↗ carries the line in its sourced section — in Esar’s wording, “The first thing I do in the morning is brush my teeth and sharpen my tongue” — cited to Herbert Victor Prochnow’s The New Speaker’s Treasury of Wit and Wisdom (1958), p. 322. We checked that page ourselves.

On the other side, nothing. Wikiquote’s Dorothy Parker page ↗ does not carry this line at all — not in its sourced section, not under Attributed, not under Misattributed. QI’s earliest Parker citation is a Pittsburgh Post-Gazette feature of 4 July 2006, sixty-six years after Levant.
source.excerptNote: That is Quote Investigator’s transcription ↗ of the 1940 column, misspelling included. We have not seen the newspaper page itself — it sits behind a Newspapers.com paywall — so the wording here rests on QI’s reading of it, not on ours.

source.rightsNote: The line was first published in a syndicated American newspaper column in 1940, which is after the 1930 cut-off below which US works are reliably in the public domain, so we take the conservative position and assert no public-domain status. We have not established whether the copyright in that column was renewed — renewal was required for US periodicals of that era and many were not renewed — so the true status may well be freer than stated here. We would rather understate it. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Oscar Levant
author.heading: About Oscar Levant
author.metaLine: 1906–1972 · American concert pianist, composer, actor and wit
author.bio: Oscar Levant (27 December 1906 – 14 August 1972) was an American concert pianist and composer who became far better known as a professional talker — on the radio quiz Information, Please!, in films, and on his own television shows. He built a public character out of neurosis and insult, and the self-deprecating one-liner was his stock in trade, which is exactly why a joke about sharpening your tongue sits naturally on him. It is also why his lines are so easy to lose: Levant’s fame faded, Parker’s did not, and orphaned wisecracks drift toward the name people still recognise.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The line travels as one of Dorothy Parker’s. It is not hers, and the paper trail is unusually clean about when the swap happened.

items.why: Every citation QI locates in the 1940s names Levant. The earliest printing it finds crediting Parker is a Pittsburgh Post-Gazette feature of 4 July 2006 — sixty-six years after the first Levant citation. Her Wikiquote page ↗ does not list the line at all.
Quote Investigator ↗ concludes that “Oscar Levant can be credited with the statement in the 1940 citation,” and Wikiquote sources a variant to him ↗ independently.

misattribution.truthLine: Levant said it; Parker inherited it sixty-six years later, for no better reason than that she is the wit people remember — see Quote Investigator’s trail ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Levant and Parker were selling the same product in the same decades: the cruel, fast, quotable remark. He did it on radio and screen, she did it in print and at the Algonquin. When a joke of that shape comes loose from its author, it does not drift at random — it drifts toward whichever wit is still famous.

That is the whole mechanism here. The 1940s press was unanimous about Levant; nobody attached Parker’s name for another sixty-six years. By then Levant was a half-remembered figure and Parker was a brand, and a brand is a magnet.
detailsBody: One detail is worth keeping, because it is the kind of thing that makes an attribution stick or slip: in the first printing the name is misspelled “Lavant.” A misspelt byline is a weak handle. It makes a line harder to search for, harder to index, and easier to detach from its author — and a detached line goes looking for a better-known home.
We have not seen the 1940 page ourselves; it is paywalled at Newspapers.com. QI reports having read it, and we cite QI as the reader rather than claiming the newspaper as ours.
context.pull: Orphaned wisecracks drift toward the name people still recognise.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator dates the earliest printing to the Santa Cruz Evening News of 26 September 1940 in Erskine Johnson’s Hollywood Today column (surname set as "Lavant"), lists Winchell 1941, Sheilah Graham 1946, Reader’s Digest 1946 and Esar 1949 as further citations naming Levant, gives a Pittsburgh Post-Gazette feature of 4 July 2006 as the earliest Parker credit, and concludes the Parker linkage was spurious.

Wikiquote’s Oscar Levant page carries "The first thing I do in the morning is brush my teeth and sharpen my tongue" in its sourced Quotes section, cited to Herbert Victor Prochnow, The New Speaker’s Treasury of Wit and Wisdom (1958), p. 322.
Wikiquote’s Dorothy Parker page does not contain this quip in any section, including Attributed and Misattributed.
Wikipedia gives Oscar Levant as an American pianist, composer, author, actor and comedian, born 27 December 1906 and died 14 August 1972.
Wikipedia gives Dorothy Parker as an American poet, writer and critic, 1893–1967.
